content: The enzyme CYP3A4 plays a critical role in the metabolism of many drugs. When co-administering drugs that induce CYP3A4 with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, plasma concentrations of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir may decrease, potentially leading to a loss of therapeutic effect. Close monitoring is recommended. Paclitaxel can increase the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by reducing its metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised during co-administration. When glecaprevir/pibrentasvir is co-administered with OATP1B1/OATP1B3 inhibitors, the plasma concentrations of drugs that are substrates of these transporters may increase. This can lead to elevated levels or effects of paclitaxel, mediated by P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Paliperidone can increase the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters, and vice versa. Caution and close monitoring are required. Pantoprazole may increase the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by decreasing its metabolism. Similarly, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir can increase the levels or effects of pantoprazole. Caution and monitoring are advised. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir may elevate plasma concentrations of P-gp and BCRP substrates. Pazopanib, for example, can increase glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by reducing its metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. Pentobarbital and phenobarbital can decrease the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This may result in reduced therapeutic efficacy. Caution and close monitoring are advised. Phenytoin significantly reduces glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative drugs should be considered, as co-administration is not recommended. Pioglitazone can increase glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by reducing its metabolism. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Pitavastatin levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir due to OATP1B1 inhibition, raising the risk of myopathy, including rhabdomyolysis. Use the lowest approved dose of pitavastatin and monitor closely. Pomalidomide levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are advised. Posaconazole can increase glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir can elevate posaconazole levels via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and close monitoring are required. Pravastatin levels may increase due to OATP1B1 inhibition by glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, raising the risk of myopathy. If co-administered, reduce the pravastatin dose by 50% and monitor closely. Prazosin levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Prednisone levels may decrease when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are advised. Pretomanid may increase glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels. Increased monitoring for drug-related adverse effects is recommended when co-administered with sensitive OATP1B3 substrates. Primidone reduces glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is not recommended; alternative drugs should be used. Natural progesterone levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are advised. Propafenone and propranolol levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Quinidine and quinine levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are advised. Ranolazine levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Regorafenib levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by reducing its metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Repaglinide levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir due to OATP1B1/OATP1B3 inhibition. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Rifampin significantly reduces glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by inducing CYP3A4 and P-gp metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the potential for therapeutic failure. Rifaximin levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are advised. Rimegepant levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Alternative drugs should be considered. Riociguat levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Risperidone levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are advised. Ritonavir significantly increases glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by reducing its metabolism. Co-administration is not recommended due to the risk of adverse effects. Rolapitant levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by reducing its metabolism. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Rosiglitazone levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by reducing its metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Rosuvastatin levels may increase due to OATP1B1 inhibition by glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, raising the risk of myopathy. Do not exceed 10 mg/day of rosuvastatin if co-administered. Rucaparib levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Adjust dosages of CYP3A4 substrates as clinically indicated. Safinamide levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by reducing its metabolism. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Sarecycline levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Monitor for toxicities and consider dosage adjustments. Saxagliptin levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are advised. Seladelpar levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. Monitor for adverse effects if co-administered with BCRP inhibitors. Selexipag levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by reducing its metabolism. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Silodosin levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are advised. Simvastatin levels may increase due to OATP1B1 inhibition by glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, raising the risk of myopathy. Co-administration is not recommended. Sirolimus levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are necessary. Sitagliptin levels may increase when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution and monitoring are advised. Sotorasib levels may decrease when co-administered with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Alternative drugs should be considered. St. John’s Wort significantly reduces glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by inducing CYP3A4 and P-gp metabolism. Co-administration is not recommended due to the potential for therapeutic failure. Stiripentol can increase or decrease glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor closely and consider dosage adjustments for CYP3A4 substrates.
